_comment: Preguntas ORIGINALES tipo NIE del capítulo 3.6. No son preguntas reales del examen. Comprueba con tu edición 2027.

questions.scenario: Which best describes handling stolen goods under s. 22 Theft Act 1968?
options: Otherwise than in the course of stealing, knowing or believing goods to be stolen, dishonestly receiving them or undertaking/assisting in their retention, removal, disposal or realisation by or for another, or arranging to do so

questions.scenario: What is the maximum sentence for handling stolen goods (⚠ check)?
RAY buys a new laptop worth £1,000 for £50 from a stranger in a pub who says 'don't ask questions'. RAY says he suspected it might be stolen but wasn't sure. Which is correct?
options: Suspicion alone is not enough; the jury must find he knew or believed (no other reasonable conclusion)
He is guilty because the price was low
He is not guilty because he paid
explanations: Correct: R v Hall; R v Grainge.

questions.scenario: What does 'believing' mean for handling (R v Hall (1985))?
options: 'I can't say for certain, but there can be no other reasonable conclusion in the light of all the circumstances'

questions.scenario: SUE lets her brother hide stolen bicycles in her garage, knowing they are stolen. Which form of handling?
options: Undertaking or assisting in their retention for the benefit of another

questions.scenario: A man agrees by text to buy a stolen car tomorrow, knowing it's stolen. The deal never happens. Has he handled?
options: Yes – arranging to receive is a form of handling

questions.scenario: A burglar is still inside a house passing items through the window to an accomplice outside. Is the accomplice a handler?
options: Only if he keeps the items
Not if this is 'in the course of the stealing' – he may be a party to burglary/theft instead
questions.manualRef: Blackstone's 2027 · 3.6 · Otherwise than in the course of stealing

questions.scenario: Police recover a stolen parcel and then allow it to be delivered to the suspect as planned. Can he be convicted of handling stolen goods?
options: Yes, the goods are still stolen
Generally no – the goods ceased to be stolen when in lawful custody; consider attempted handling
questions.manualRef: Blackstone's 2027 · 3.6 · Goods ceasing to be stolen

questions.scenario: Goods obtained by which of these can be 'stolen goods' for handling?
A burglar sells stolen jewellery and gives the cash to his girlfriend, who knows its origin. Can the cash be stolen goods?
options: Yes – goods representing the stolen goods can be stolen goods

questions.scenario: A man buys a car in good faith; later he learns it was stolen and sells it on for his own benefit. Is he handling 'for the benefit of another'?
options: No – a purchaser selling for his own benefit is not acting for another (R v Bloxham)
explanations: The buyer isn't 'another' in this sense.

questions.scenario: Is the test for 'knowing or believing' objective or subjective?
options: Objective – what a reasonable person would believe
Subjective – what the defendant actually knew or believed

questions.scenario: Under s. 27(3), evidence that the defendant handled other stolen goods within what period may be admitted to prove knowledge/belief?
Under s. 27(3)(b), a conviction for theft or handling within how many years may be admitted (with notice)?
A woman lies to police, saying a stolen TV in her flat was a gift, to stop it being found to be stolen and help her son. Which is correct?
options: She may be assisting in the retention of stolen goods for the benefit of another
explanations: Lying to conceal can be assisting.

questions.scenario: A man simply uses a stolen bike that his friend left at his house, without hiding it or helping keep it. Is mere use enough for assisting in retention?
options: Not by itself – there must be something done to assist retention
Yes, if he rides it daily
explanations: Painting to disguise it might be assisting.

questions.scenario: Which mental element besides knowledge/belief is required for handling?
A thief, a week after stealing a phone, sells it to a friend. Can the thief be a handler of that phone?
options: Only if he stole it again
Yes – after the theft is complete, a thief can handle the goods (e.g. disposal for another's benefit)
Only if he is paid in goods

questions.scenario: Dishonestly retaining a wrongful credit is an offence under…
Goods stolen abroad and brought into England are…
options: only stolen if the owner is British
stolen goods if the act was an offence where committed and would have been theft/blackmail/fraud in England

questions.scenario: Is handling stolen goods triable either way?
A pawnbroker accepts jewellery, believing it is stolen, and then sells it to a customer. Which forms of handling may apply?
Which of these is NOT a form of handling in s. 22?
options: Reporting the goods to the police

questions.scenario: Why is the maximum for handling higher than for theft?
options: Handlers create a market that encourages theft
It's a mistake in the law

questions.scenario: A suspect says: 'I thought the phones might be stolen, but I didn't want to know.' What might this support?
options: Belief, if the jury finds no other reasonable conclusion; deliberately not asking can be evidence

questions.scenario: The owner of a stolen car loses the right to restitution (e.g. by a lawful sale abroad). What happens to the goods' status?
Does 'receiving' require the goods to be received for the benefit of another?
options: No – the 'by or for the benefit of another' words apply to the undertaking/assisting forms

questions.scenario: A delivery driver knowingly transports stolen TVs for a gang. Which form?
options: Undertaking/assisting in removal for the benefit of another

questions.scenario: Which statement about 'realisation' is correct?
options: It means converting the goods into money or value, e.g. selling

questions.scenario: A man is found with a stolen phone. There is no evidence of when or how he got it. Which charge may be harder to prove than theft?
options: Handling requires proof of knowing/believing and 'otherwise than in the course of stealing'; prosecutors may charge both in the alternative
